title: China’s Industrial “Rainforest” Offers Insights for the Global South
text:
China’s Industrial “Rainforest” Offers Insights for the Global South

China Global South Project

CN-STR/AFP/Getty Images

The following excerpt is from a column published in China Global South Project on August 27, 2026, written by Li Shuo, Director of ASPI's China Climate Hub and a Senior Fellow at ASPI's Center for China Analysis.Energiewende is a German word no international energy researcher can avoid. Coined in the 1980s and entering mainstream political discourse in the early 2000s, the term describes Germany’s ambitious project to transform its energy system around clean power. Yet these days, the word is heard less in its home country. In a curious twist, the vision embodied by Energiewende is being realized thousands of miles away—in China.In Zhanjiang, a southern Chinese industrial city, BASF’s sprawling chemical complex offers a striking illustration of this paradox. The €8.7 billion investment by the German chemical giant is one of the largest foreign investments in China and a world-scale chemical production hub, marrying the German giant’s technical expertise with China’s manufacturing prowess.Most strikingly, the complex is a massive consumer of electricity—and in a distinctly Energiewende spirit, BASF says core production is powered by 100 percent renewable electricity.What underpins BASF’s ambition is an energy system that China has spent decades building: abundant, cheap, rapidly deployable, and increasingly clean. This unusual combination is beginning to redefine the economics of industrial production in China, giving it an advantage that extends far beyond low-end manufacturing.Read the full column here.
